questions.title: Site of aqueous humour secretion
questions.question: Aqueous humour is secreted by:

explanations.A: Incorrect. The angle of the anterior chamber is the drainage route for aqueous, not a secretory structure.
explanations.B: Correct. Aqueous humour is actively secreted by the epithelium of the ciliary body into the posterior chamber. From there it passes through the pupil into the anterior chamber and drains at the angle. The ciliary body is therefore the source of aqueous, and the balance between its secretion and drainage sets the intraocular pressure.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The posterior surface of the iris borders the posterior chamber but does not secrete aqueous.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The lens is an avascular refractive structure and plays no part in aqueous secretion.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the ciliary body as the site of aqueous humour secretion.

questions.title: Route of aqueous humour drainage
questions.question: Aqueous humour is drained through:

explanations.A: Correct. Aqueous humour drains out of the eye at the angle of the anterior chamber, passing through the trabecular meshwork into the canal of Schlemm and then to the episcleral veins. Obstruction of this outflow pathway raises the intraocular pressure and causes glaucoma. The angle is thus the exit route, in contrast to the ciliary body which produces the fluid.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The ciliary body secretes aqueous humour; it is the site of production, not drainage.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The posterior surface of the iris is not a drainage structure.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The lens has no role in aqueous drainage.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the anterior chamber angle as the route of aqueous humour drainage.

questions.title: Chamber where aqueous humour is produced
questions.question: Aqueous humour is produced in which chamber of the eye:

explanations.A: Incorrect. The anterior chamber receives aqueous through the pupil; it is not the site of production.
explanations.B: Correct. The ciliary body secretes aqueous humour into the posterior chamber, the space behind the iris and in front of the lens and zonules. The fluid then flows forward through the pupil into the anterior chamber and drains at the angle. Production into the posterior chamber is therefore the first step of the aqueous circulation.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The vitreous cavity contains vitreous gel, not freshly secreted aqueous.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The trabecular meshwork is a drainage structure at the angle, not a chamber.

questions.learning_objective: State that aqueous humour is produced into the posterior chamber.

questions.title: The outer coat of the eye
questions.question: The outer coat of the eye:

options.A: Is formed of cornea, sclera and iris
options.C: Cornea does not have a refractive function
options.D: Protects against the invasion of micro-organisms

explanations.A: Incorrect. The outer fibrous coat is formed of cornea and sclera only; the iris belongs to the middle (uveal) coat.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The outer coat is protective but the cornea is also the eye's main refractive element, so it is not only protective.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The cornea provides about 43 diopters, the largest single refractive contribution of the eye.
explanations.D: Correct. The outer (fibrous) coat is the cornea and sclera and acts as a tough protective barrier against mechanical injury and microbial invasion. An intact corneal epithelium and dense scleral collagen resist penetration by organisms. The cornea additionally serves a major refractive function, so the coat is both protective and optical.

questions.learning_objective: Describe the protective role of the outer fibrous coat (cornea and sclera).

questions.title: The middle coat of the eye
questions.question: The middle coat of the eye:

options.C: Consists of the iris, ciliary body and retina
options.D: Is also called the neurosensory coat

explanations.A: Correct. The middle coat is the uvea, made of the iris, ciliary body and choroid, and it is the vascular coat that supplies blood to the eye. It is heavily pigmented, but its defining feature relative to the other options is that it is the vascular tunic. The neurosensory coat is the retina, which lies internal to the uvea.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The uvea is indeed pigmented, but this is not the single best answer because being the vascular coat is its defining characteristic here.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The uvea is iris, ciliary body and choroid; the retina is the separate inner coat.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The neurosensory coat is the retina, not the uvea.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the uvea as the vascular middle coat of the eye.

questions.title: Opening of the nasolacrimal duct
questions.question: The nasolacrimal duct opens in:

explanations.A: Incorrect. The superior meatus receives the posterior ethmoidal sinus, not the nasolacrimal duct.
explanations.B: Correct. The nasolacrimal duct carries tears from the lacrimal sac and opens into the inferior nasal meatus beneath the inferior turbinate. This is why tears ultimately reach the nose, and why nasolacrimal obstruction causes watering (epiphora). Its opening is guarded by the valve of Hasner.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The middle meatus drains most of the paranasal sinuses (frontal, maxillary, anterior ethmoid), not the tear duct.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The duct opens into the inferior meatus of the nasal cavity, not directly into the nasopharynx.

questions.learning_objective: State that the nasolacrimal duct drains into the inferior nasal meatus.

questions.title: Epithelium covering the cornea
questions.question: The cornea is covered by:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Keratinization would opacify the surface; the cornea must stay clear, so it is not keratinized.
explanations.B: Correct. The corneal surface is covered by non-keratinized stratified squamous epithelium. The absence of keratin keeps the epithelium optically clear and smooth, and it is kept moist by the tear film. This epithelium regenerates rapidly from limbal stem cells after injury.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Pseudo-stratified columnar epithelium lines the respiratory tract, not the cornea.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The corneal epithelium is squamous, not columnar.

questions.learning_objective: State the epithelial type covering the cornea.

questions.title: Factors of corneal transparency (except)
questions.question: Corneal transparency is due to all of the following factors EXCEPT:

options.A: Compact arrangement of corneal stromal fibres

explanations.A: Incorrect (this IS a factor). The regular, compact lamellar arrangement of stromal collagen minimises light scatter and is essential for transparency.
explanations.B: Incorrect (this IS a factor). Avascularity keeps the cornea clear; corneal neovascularisation reduces transparency.
explanations.C: Correct. Myelinated nerve fibres are NOT a factor in corneal transparency. Corneal nerves in fact lose their myelin sheaths shortly after entering the cornea, precisely because myelin would scatter light. Transparency instead depends on avascularity, the regular stromal lamellae, the non-keratinized epithelium and the endothelial dehydration pump.
explanations.D: Incorrect (this IS a factor). The smooth non-keratinized epithelium provides a clear refracting surface.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise that myelinated nerve fibres are not among the factors maintaining corneal transparency.

questions.title: A property of the cornea
questions.question: The cornea has:

explanations.A: Incorrect. The cornea has five layers (epithelium, Bowman, stroma, Descemet, endothelium), not three.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The cornea is avascular; its clarity depends on the absence of blood vessels.
explanations.C: Correct. The corneal endothelium contains active metabolic pumps that continuously move fluid out of the stroma (deturgescence), keeping the cornea relatively dehydrated and transparent. Endothelial failure lets the stroma swell and cloud. This active pumping is a defining physiological property of the cornea.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The stromal collagen fibres are regularly and compactly arranged, which is why the cornea is clear.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The cornea is kept relatively dehydrated by the endothelial pump; excess water content causes oedema and opacity.

questions.learning_objective: Identify active endothelial pumps as a key property of the cornea.

questions.title: Refractive power of the crystalline lens
questions.question: The refractive power of the eye lens is about … in diopters:

explanations.A: Incorrect. This underestimates the resting power of the lens as taught here.
explanations.B: Correct. The crystalline lens contributes about 20 diopters to the eye's resting refractive power. This is considerably less than the cornea, which provides roughly 43 diopters and is the eye's main refractive element. The lens can increase its power further during accommodation by changing shape.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Thirty diopters overestimates the lens power and approaches the combined optics of the eye.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Forty diopters is closer to the corneal power, not the lens.

questions.learning_objective: Recall the approximate resting refractive power of the crystalline lens.

questions.title: Corneal layers (except)
questions.question: The cornea is made of the following layers EXCEPT:

explanations.A: Incorrect (this IS a corneal layer). Bowman membrane lies beneath the epithelium.
explanations.B: Incorrect (this IS a corneal layer). The stroma is the thick middle layer of the cornea.
explanations.C: Correct. Bruch's membrane is NOT a corneal layer; it is part of the choroid/retinal pigment epithelium complex in the posterior segment. The cornea is made of epithelium, Bowman membrane, stroma, Descemet membrane and endothelium. The similar name to Bowman's membrane is the trap.
explanations.D: Incorrect (this IS a corneal layer). The endothelium is the innermost corneal layer.

questions.learning_objective: Distinguish the corneal layers from Bruch membrane of the posterior segment.

questions.title: Factors affecting corneal transparency (except)
questions.question: Factors affecting the corneal transparency include the following EXCEPT:

explanations.A: Incorrect (this IS a factor). Avascularity keeps the cornea clear.
explanations.B: Incorrect (this IS a factor). The endothelial pump dehydrates the stroma to maintain clarity.
explanations.C: Incorrect (this IS a factor). Regular lamellar arrangement of stromal collagen minimises scatter.
explanations.D: Correct. A keratinized epithelium is NOT a factor maintaining corneal transparency; on the contrary, the corneal epithelium is non-keratinized, and keratinization would scatter light and opacify the surface. The true maintaining factors are avascularity, the endothelial pump and the regular stromal lamellae. So keratinization is the odd one out.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise that keratinized epithelium is not a factor preserving corneal transparency.

questions.title: Components of the uveal tract (except)
questions.question: The uveal tract is composed of the following EXCEPT:

explanations.A: Incorrect (this IS part of the uvea). The iris is the anterior part of the uveal tract.
explanations.B: Incorrect (this IS part of the uvea). The ciliary body is the middle part.
explanations.C: Correct. The retina is NOT part of the uveal tract. The uvea is the vascular middle coat, composed of the iris, ciliary body and choroid. The retina is the separate innermost neurosensory coat, lying internal to the choroid.
explanations.D: Incorrect (this IS part of the uvea). The choroid is the posterior part of the uveal tract.

questions.learning_objective: List the components of the uveal tract and exclude the retina.

questions.title: Boundaries of the posterior chamber
questions.question: The posterior chamber is the space between:

options.A: The crystalline lens and the iris
options.B: The crystalline lens and the vitreous
options.D: The ciliary body and the crystalline lens

explanations.A: Correct. The posterior chamber is the space bounded in front by the iris and behind by the crystalline lens and its zonules. Aqueous humour secreted by the ciliary body first fills this chamber before passing through the pupil. It should not be confused with the anterior chamber, which lies between the cornea and the iris.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The space in front of the vitreous behind the lens is not the posterior chamber.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The iris-to-cornea space is the anterior chamber.
explanations.D: Incorrect. This describes only part of the boundary; the chamber is defined between iris and lens.

questions.learning_objective: Define the boundaries of the posterior chamber of the eye.

questions.title: Parts of the conjunctiva (except)
questions.question: The conjunctiva is formed of the following parts EXCEPT:

explanations.A: Incorrect (this IS a conjunctival part). The palpebral conjunctiva lines the inner eyelids.
explanations.B: Incorrect (this IS a conjunctival part). The bulbar conjunctiva covers the sclera.
explanations.C: Incorrect (this IS a conjunctival part). The fornices are the reflections between palpebral and bulbar conjunctiva.
explanations.D: Correct. The tarsus is NOT a part of the conjunctiva; it is the dense fibrous plate that gives the eyelid its shape. The conjunctiva is formed of the palpebral part, the bulbar part and the fornices. The palpebral conjunctiva merely lines the tarsus, which itself is eyelid connective tissue.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the parts of the conjunctiva and exclude the tarsus.

questions.title: Investigation versus routine examination
questions.question: The following is an investigation, not a part of the ophthalmic examination:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Autorefractometry is a standard part of refractive assessment in the eye examination.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Indirect ophthalmoscopy is a core bedside method of fundus examination.
explanations.C: Correct. Optical coherence tomography (OCT) is a dedicated imaging investigation that produces cross-sectional images of the retina and optic nerve. It is an ancillary special investigation rather than a component of the basic bedside ophthalmic examination. The other options are routine examination steps performed with standard clinic equipment.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Tonometry (measuring intraocular pressure) is a routine part of the examination.

questions.learning_objective: Classify OCT as an ancillary investigation rather than a routine examination step.

questions.title: Abnormal pupillary reflex colours (false statement)
questions.question: One of the following statements is false:

options.A: A white reflex may indicate mature cataract
options.C: A black reflex is seen in vitreous haemorrhage
options.D: A yellow reflex points to endophthalmitis

explanations.A: Incorrect (this statement is TRUE). A white pupillary reflex (leukocoria) can be due to a mature cataract or retinoblastoma.
explanations.B: Correct (this is the FALSE statement). There is no recognised blue pupillary reflex that indicates glaucoma. Glaucoma is diagnosed by a raised intraocular pressure with optic-disc cupping and visual-field loss, not by a reflex colour. The other three reflex colours are valid diagnostic clues.
explanations.C: Incorrect (this statement is TRUE). A dark or black reflex can be seen when vitreous haemorrhage blocks the fundal glow.
explanations.D: Incorrect (this statement is TRUE). A yellowish reflex may point to endophthalmitis (a purulent exudate behind the lens).

questions.learning_objective: Interpret the abnormal pupillary reflex colours and reject the false blue-reflex/glaucoma pairing.

questions.title: The orbit (true statement)
questions.question: Regarding the orbit:

options.B: The orbit is closely related to the paranasal sinuses
options.C: The orbit communicates with the skull via 4 main ports
options.D: The commonest cause of orbital cellulitis is conjunctivitis

explanations.A: Incorrect. The orbit is a four-walled pyramid (roof, floor, medial and lateral walls), not a three-walled cone.
explanations.B: Correct. The bony orbit is closely related to the paranasal sinuses: the ethmoid sinus lies medially, the frontal sinus above and the maxillary sinus below. This intimate relation is clinically important because it explains why paranasal sinusitis is the commonest cause of orbital cellulitis. Infection spreads from the adjacent sinuses across the thin orbital walls.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The orbit communicates with the cranial cavity mainly through the optic canal and the superior orbital fissure, not four main ports.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The commonest cause of orbital cellulitis is spread from the paranasal sinuses, not conjunctivitis.

questions.learning_objective: Describe the close anatomical relation of the orbit to the paranasal sinuses.

questions.title: Anatomy of the cornea (true statement)
questions.question: Regarding the anatomy of the cornea:

options.A: Cornea is made up of 7 layers
options.B: The stroma is made of collagen fibres arranged in lamellae
options.C: Corneal transparency is due to vascularity
options.D: Active endothelial pump plays a minor role in transparency of cornea

explanations.A: Incorrect. The cornea is classically described as having five layers (a sixth, Dua's layer, is debated), not seven.
explanations.B: Correct. The corneal stroma, the thickest layer, is composed of collagen fibrils arranged into regular parallel lamellae. This precise, uniform spacing of the fibrils minimises light scattering and is a key reason the cornea is transparent. Together with avascularity and the endothelial pump, the lamellar stroma keeps the cornea clear.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Transparency depends on the cornea being avascular; vascularisation reduces clarity.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The active endothelial pump plays a major, not minor, role in maintaining transparency.

questions.learning_objective: Describe the lamellar collagen organisation of the corneal stroma.

questions.title: Hirschberg test estimation of deviation
questions.question: If the corneal light reflex is 2 mm temporal to the pupil in the right eye, the deviation is estimated to be:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Ten prism diopters would correspond to roughly 0.7 mm of reflex displacement, less than observed.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Twenty prism diopters corresponds to about 1.3 mm, still short of the 2 mm seen.
explanations.C: Correct. In the Hirschberg corneal light reflex test each 1 mm of reflex displacement corresponds to approximately 15 prism diopters of ocular deviation, so a 2 mm displacement equals about 30 prism diopters. A reflex displaced temporally means the visual axis is turned inward, i.e. an esotropia. Hence a 2 mm temporal reflex indicates roughly 30 diopters of esotropia.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Forty prism diopters would need about 2.7 mm of displacement, more than observed.

questions.learning_objective: Estimate the angle of strabismus from the Hirschberg corneal reflex displacement.

questions.title: Methods of fundus examination (except)
questions.question: Methods of fundus examination include the following EXCEPT:

explanations.A: Incorrect (this IS a fundus method). Slit-lamp biomicroscopy with accessory lenses examines the fundus.
explanations.B: Incorrect (this IS a fundus method). Direct ophthalmoscopy gives a magnified upright view of the fundus.
explanations.C: Incorrect (this IS a fundus method). Indirect ophthalmoscopy gives a wide-field inverted view of the fundus.
explanations.D: Correct. Retinoscopy is NOT a method of fundus examination; it is an objective technique for measuring the refractive error of the eye by observing the movement of a light reflex. The genuine fundus-examination methods are direct and indirect ophthalmoscopy and slit-lamp biomicroscopy with lenses. Retinoscopy assesses refraction, not retinal detail.

questions.learning_objective: Distinguish fundus-examination techniques from retinoscopy.

questions.title: What confrontation field testing detects
questions.question: Visual field testing using the confrontation method can diagnose:

explanations.A: Incorrect. An enlarged blind spot is a subtle defect detectable only by formal perimetry, not confrontation.
explanations.B: Incorrect. A small paracentral scotoma is too fine for the crude confrontation test.
explanations.C: Correct. The confrontation method is a gross bedside comparison of the patient's visual field with the examiner's, so it detects large defects such as a hemianopia. It is not sensitive enough to reveal small or shallow defects, which require formal perimetry. Confrontation is therefore a screening test for major field loss such as that from a chiasmal or retrochiasmal lesion.
explanations.D: Incorrect. A nasal step is a fine glaucomatous field defect that needs perimetry, not confrontation.

questions.learning_objective: State what visual-field defects the confrontation method can and cannot detect.

questions.title: Orbit and paranasal sinus relations (false statement)
questions.question: Regarding the paranasal sinuses, the following is true EXCEPT:

options.A: The ethmoid sinus is located medially
options.B: The roof of the orbit separates the orbit from the frontal sinus
options.C: The lateral wall separates the orbit from the sphenoid sinus
options.D: The floor separates the orbit from the maxillary sinus

explanations.A: Incorrect (this statement is TRUE). The ethmoid sinus lies along the medial wall of the orbit.
explanations.B: Incorrect (this statement is TRUE). The orbital roof separates the orbit from the frontal sinus (and anterior cranial fossa).
explanations.C: Correct (this is the FALSE statement). The lateral wall is the thickest orbital wall and is NOT related to the sphenoid sinus; the sphenoid sinus is related posteriorly to the medial wall/orbital apex. Sinus relations of the orbit are with the roof (frontal), floor (maxillary) and medial wall (ethmoid and, posteriorly, sphenoid). The lateral wall separates the orbit from the temporal and middle cranial fossae, not a sinus.
explanations.D: Incorrect (this statement is TRUE). The orbital floor separates the orbit from the maxillary sinus, which is why blow-out fractures involve the maxillary antrum.

questions.learning_objective: Describe the relations of the orbital walls to the paranasal sinuses.

questions.title: Suspensory apparatus of the lens
questions.question: The crystalline lens is suspended from the ciliary body processes by:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Lens sutures are the Y-shaped junctions of lens fibres inside the lens, not its suspensory apparatus.
explanations.B: Correct. The crystalline lens is suspended from the ciliary body processes by the zonular fibres (zonules of Zinn), a ring of fine fibres running from the ciliary body to the lens equator. These zonules hold the lens in position and transmit the pull of the ciliary muscle during accommodation. Weakness or rupture of the zonules causes lens subluxation.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The lens capsule is the elastic envelope of the lens itself, not the suspensory ligament.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Lens fibres are the internal cellular substance of the lens.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the zonules as the suspensory apparatus of the lens.

questions.title: Structures of the anterior chamber angle (except)
questions.question: The following is not a structure of the anterior chamber angle:

explanations.A: Incorrect (this IS an angle structure). The trabecular meshwork is the main drainage tissue at the angle.
explanations.B: Incorrect (this IS an angle structure). The scleral spur is a landmark of the angle to which the ciliary muscle attaches.
explanations.C: Correct. The retinal pigment epithelium is NOT a structure of the anterior chamber angle; it lies in the posterior segment beneath the neurosensory retina. The angle structures seen on gonioscopy are Schwalbe line, the trabecular meshwork, the scleral spur, the ciliary body band and the iris root. The RPE is far removed from the drainage angle.
explanations.D: Incorrect (this IS an angle structure). Schwalbe line marks the peripheral termination of Descemet membrane at the angle.

questions.learning_objective: List the structures of the anterior chamber angle and exclude the retinal pigment epithelium.

questions.title: Contents of the superior orbital fissure
questions.question: The superior orbital fissure transmits:

options.B: Ophthalmic branch of the trigeminal nerve

explanations.A: Incorrect. The ophthalmic artery passes through the optic canal, not the superior orbital fissure.
explanations.B: Correct. The superior orbital fissure transmits the oculomotor (III), trochlear (IV) and abducent (VI) nerves, the ophthalmic (first) division of the trigeminal nerve (V1) and the superior ophthalmic vein. The ophthalmic division of the trigeminal is therefore one of its contents. The optic nerve and ophthalmic artery instead traverse the optic canal.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The optic nerve passes through the optic canal, not the superior orbital fissure.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The central retinal artery travels within the optic nerve through the optic canal.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve as a structure of the superior orbital fissure.
